cues.x: The Big Short, by Michael Lewis.
Let me start with a man in a windowless office in San Jose, California, in 2005, sitting alone in the dark with the door closed and the lights off, reading mortgage bond prospectuses.
His name is Michael Burry.
He is a doctor by training, a neurology resident who quit medicine to run a hedge fund.

He has one glass eye, having lost the other to a childhood cancer, and he will tell you that the glass eye is why he has never been much good at reading faces or holding a conversation, because people always seem to be looking at the wrong part of him.
He works with the lights off and heavy metal playing.

He is, at this point, running a fund called Scion Capital out of an unfashionable office with a handful of employees, and he is doing something that, as far as anyone can tell, nobody else in the world is doing.
He is reading the documents.
A subprime mortgage bond prospectus runs to something like a hundred and thirty pages of dense legal and statistical material.

It describes exactly which loans have been packaged into the bond: what kind of borrowers, what kind of houses, what kind of interest rates, and crucially, what happens to those interest rates over time.
These documents were issued by the thousand.
They were mailed out to investors, to analysts, to ratings agencies, to everybody.

And Michael Burry became convinced, on the evidence, that he was the only person outside the legal departments who actually read them, because the things he found in them were so obviously alarming that if anyone else had read them, somebody would have said something.
What he found was this.
A huge and growing proportion of American mortgages were being made to people who could not possibly repay them, on terms specifically designed to disguise that fact for two years.
The loans carried a low fixed teaser rate for the first two years, then reset to a much higher floating rate.
As long as house prices kept rising, the borrower could refinance before the reset and everybody got paid.
The moment prices stopped rising, the refinancing stopped working, the resets landed, and the borrowers defaulted en masse.
And Burry did the arithmetic on when.
The loans made in 2005 would reset in 2007.
Not "eventually".
Not "at some point in the cycle".
2007. He circled the date.
That is the book.

Michael Lewis takes one of the most complicated financial events in history and tells it as the story of a handful of socially awkward, difficult, frequently unpleasant outsiders who noticed something enormous that thousands of well paid insiders somehow did not, and who then had to endure two years of being told they were idiots while being right.
Lewis opens with a confession about himself, and it is worth hearing because it sets his angle.
In the late 1980s he worked as a bond salesman at Salomon Brothers, and he wrote a book about it called Liar's Poker, which was intended as a farewell to an era of absurd excess.
He thought he was writing an obituary.
Instead, for the next twenty years, he received letters from college students asking whether he had any more tips, because they had read his exposé of a corrupt and idiotic culture as a how to guide.
The excess did not end.
It multiplied by a factor Lewis could not have imagined.
So he came back to find out what had happened, and this book is the answer.
His way in was a woman called Meredith Whitney.

On the thirty first of October 2007, Whitney, then a relatively obscure analyst at Oppenheimer, published a report saying that Citigroup, the largest bank in America, had mismanaged its affairs so badly that it would have to cut its dividend or effectively go bust.
She was thirty something, largely unknown, and she was making a claim about a bank whose leadership had just told the world everything was fine.
The market lost something like three hundred and ninety billion dollars of value that day.
Within days Citigroup cut its dividend and its chief executive resigned.
Meredith Whitney became famous, and the reason she became famous is that she had said, in public and in advance, what turned out to be true.
Lewis rang her and asked her a simple question: who else knew?
Who else saw this coming and had money on it?
She gave him a short list of names.
At the top was Steve Eisman.

So let me introduce the cast, because the pleasure of this book is that they are all, in different ways, unable to function normally in polite society, and that is precisely why they saw what they saw.

Steve Eisman was a lawyer's son from New York who had drifted into Wall Street through his parents, who were both brokers, and had become an analyst covering what the industry called specialty finance, meaning consumer lenders.
He was famous for being spectacularly, almost pathologically rude.
He interrupted people mid sentence.
He asked chief executives questions in public that no analyst asks.
He once, at a large presentation by a lending company, raised his hand and gave the presenter a zero with his fingers when asked to estimate the probability of a scenario.

Colleagues described him as having no filter whatsoever, and Lewis reports the general opinion that he was not being deliberately offensive, he simply had no functioning sense that certain things are not said.
His first assignment as a junior analyst, back in the early 1990s, had been to write a report on a subprime lender.
Nobody told him what he was supposed to conclude, and he did not know that analysts were supposed to say nice things, so he read it, thought it was rubbish, and said so.
Later, in 1997, when the first wave of subprime lending blew up, he wrote a scathing report on the whole sector, and he was right.
And in between, he had the experience that turned a sceptical analyst into a genuinely angry man.
In the early 2000s, Eisman got interested in a large consumer lender called Household International, which was selling second mortgages to ordinary people.
He obtained the sales documents, and he sat down and worked out what the loans actually cost.
The company was advertising a fixed rate loan at what looked like around seven percent.
When Eisman did the arithmetic on the actual terms, the effective interest rate the borrower was paying came out at something closer to twelve and a half percent.
The trick was in how the numbers were presented across a very long term, and Eisman's judgement was that this was not a grey area or an aggressive interpretation.
It was, in plain language, a deception aimed at people who could not do the sums.
So he went to war.
He contacted journalists.
He contacted regulators.
He testified.
He rang people who did not want to hear from him.
It took a long time, and eventually the company reached a settlement with a large group of American states of around four hundred and eighty four million dollars.

And then the piece of information that finished off whatever was left of Eisman's faith: the company was sold, and its chief executive walked away with a personal payout reported in the region of a hundred million dollars.
Eisman's conclusion, which he carried into everything that followed, was not that some individuals behave badly.

It was that the system had discovered it could make more money lending to poor people badly than to rich people well, that the penalties for being caught were a fraction of the profits, and that nobody with the power to stop it had any interest in doing so.
Then in the mid 2000s two things happened to Steve Eisman.
The first was that subprime lending came back, larger than before, dressed in new clothes.
The second was a personal catastrophe: his infant son Max died in an accident at home while a night nurse was caring for him.
Lewis handles this carefully and briefly, and notes only that afterwards Eisman changed.
Whatever restraint he had left, he no longer bothered with.
His rage found an object.
Around him was a team.

Vincent Daniel, called Vinny, a young man from Queens who had grown up without money, who had trained at an accountancy firm auditing Wall Street's books, and who therefore had the rare and valuable habit of assuming that the numbers he was given were probably a lie until proven otherwise.

And Danny Moses, the trader, superstitious and funny and deeply distrustful, whose instinct in any meeting with a Wall Street salesman was to ask himself why this person was so eager to sell him this thing.
Vinny had, back in his auditing days, been sent to look at the accounts of the subprime lenders, and he found something that stayed with him.
It was called gain on sale accounting.

When a lender made a loan and sold it on, they were permitted to book, immediately, as profit, the entire expected future stream of income from that loan, based on their own assumptions about how many borrowers would default.
Which meant that the more loans they made, the more profit they booked today, and the assumptions about defaults were essentially self certified.
A company could grow its reported earnings simply by lending more money to worse people, and the bill would not arrive for years.
Then Greg Lippmann, who is the most entertaining figure in the book and by far the most compromised.
Lippmann was a bond trader at Deutsche Bank, loud, tactless, given to telling people uncomfortable truths about themselves, and he became the great evangelist of the short.
He built a presentation, which he showed to anyone who would sit still, arguing that the entire subprime mortgage market was going to blow up, and that you could bet against it.
But Lippmann was not primarily a prophet.
He was a market maker.
He needed people on both sides.
He had put on the bet himself, and to keep it alive he needed a crowd of other people to buy it too.

So he went around Wall Street with the missionary zeal of a man who needed customers, and he was almost the only person on the street cheerfully telling institutional investors that his own bank's core product was garbage.
His killer statistic was produced by a quantitative analyst he employed named Eugene Xu, whose actual work underpinned the pitch.
Lippmann's line went like this, and it is the single most important sentence in the book: house prices do not even need to fall.
They only need to stop rising at the unnatural rate at which they have been rising, and enormous numbers of people will default.
The numbers behind it: on the pools of loans made in the middle of the decade, if house prices simply stayed flat, defaults would produce losses of somewhere around seven percent of the pool.
If prices fell by five percent, losses would run to something like seventeen percent.
And the tranches that Lippmann wanted people to bet against, the ones rated triple B, would be entirely wiped out once losses on the underlying pool reached about eight percent.
Not reduced.
Wiped out.
Zero.
Read those numbers together.
Flat house prices, which is the mildest possible outcome, produced losses of seven percent against a wipeout threshold of eight.
There was essentially no margin at all.
And nobody had ever seriously modelled falling prices, because in the historical data the agencies used, national house prices had not fallen.
And finally, the two boys in the garage.

Charlie Ledley and Jamie Mai were friends in their early thirties who started an investment company called Cornwall Capital with a hundred and ten thousand dollars in a brokerage account, operating out of a shed behind a house in Berkeley, California, and later out of a borrowed artist's studio in Greenwich Village.
They had no financial pedigree to speak of, which is exactly why their strategy worked.
Their strategy was this: they believed markets were systematically bad at pricing things that were unlikely but enormous.
Rare events.

If something had a ten percent chance of happening and the market was pricing it at one percent, you could buy the option cheaply and be wrong most of the time and still make an enormous amount of money on the occasions you were right.
So they hunted for cheap options on extreme outcomes, in any market, anywhere.
They made money on a credit card company nobody would touch, on a Korean currency bet, on an ethanol producer.
They were amateurs in the specific sense that they had not been trained out of asking obvious questions.

They were joined by Ben Hockett, an experienced trader who had worked in Tokyo, who lived in the hills above Berkeley and had a genuine, quietly held conviction that the financial system might one day simply stop, and who therefore took very seriously the question of what happens to your winning bet if the person who owes you the money no longer exists.

It was Hockett who understood that to trade with the big banks at all, Cornwall needed a proper master agreement, the legal document that lets an institution deal with you as an equal, and that getting one as a tiny fund run by two young men with no track record would be the hardest part of the whole trade.
Now, the instrument.
Because everything turns on it, let me explain what they actually bought, in plain language.
Before 2005, if you thought the housing market was going to collapse, there was no practical way to bet against it.
You could not short a mortgage bond in the ordinary way, because there was nobody to borrow it from.
The market was structurally one directional.
You could be long, or you could stay out.
What Michael Burry did, and he did it first, was go to the big banks and ask them to create something.
He wanted a credit default swap on specific subprime mortgage bonds.
A credit default swap is, functionally, an insurance policy on a bond.
You pay a small annual premium.
If the bond defaults, you get paid the face value.
Two features made this the perfect instrument.
First, the loss was strictly limited to the premiums you paid, so a small annual cost of perhaps two percent bought you exposure to the full value.
Second, and this is what made Burry's hands shake, you could buy insurance on a bond you did not own.
You could buy fire insurance on your neighbour's house.
In fact, you could buy fire insurance on your neighbour's house a hundred times over, which is precisely what the market eventually did.
In 2005 Burry went round the banks asking for this.
Most of them did not understand what he wanted.
Deutsche Bank and Goldman Sachs eventually agreed to write the contracts.
And here is the detail that shows you Burry's edge: he did not want a bet on the market generally.
He had read the prospectuses, so he specified individual bonds, hand picked because they were stuffed with the very worst loans from the very worst lenders.
Adjustable rate mortgages.
No documentation loans, where the borrower simply stated their income and nobody checked.
Loans from the lenders he had identified as the most aggressive.
He was going into a shop and asking for insurance, by name, on the specific houses that were already smouldering.
And the banks sold it to him at the standard price, because their models did not distinguish between one triple B tranche and another.
To the machine, a bond was a bond and a rating was a rating.
Before I go further, let me build you the picture of a mortgage bond, because if you can see this shape in your head, the rest of the book unlocks.
Imagine a tower with maybe fifteen floors.
At the bottom of the tower, underneath it, is a pool of a few thousand actual home loans, made to actual people.
Every month those people send in their mortgage payments, and that money flows into the tower.
Here is the rule.
The money fills the tower from the top floor down.
The people who own the top floor get paid first, every month, before anybody else gets a penny.
Then whatever is left flows to the next floor down, then the next, and so on to the bottom.
Now flip it.
When borrowers stop paying, the losses do not come off the top.
They eat the tower from the bottom up.
The ground floor is wiped out first, then the first floor, then the second.
So the bottom floors are dangerous and pay high interest, and the top floors are safe and pay low interest.
The bottom floors were rated triple B, the ones that vanish at the first sign of trouble.
The top floors were rated triple A, and were treated by the entire financial world as being about as risky as lending money to the American government.
Michael Burry's insight was to buy insurance on the bottom floors, the triple B tranches, of the specific towers whose foundations were the rottenest.

Cornwall Capital's smarter and later insight was that the whole building was standing on a single foundation, and that if the ground floor went, the penthouse was coming down too, just a bit more slowly, and that insurance on the penthouse could be bought for almost nothing because everybody was looking at the rating rather than at the foundation.
Hold that tower in your mind, because Wall Street was about to do something extraordinary with the floors nobody wanted.
Which brings us to the ratings agencies, and to the part of the book that should make you angry.
Moody's and Standard and Poor's were paid by the banks whose bonds they rated.
That conflict is well known.

But Lewis shows you something more damning, which is that the agencies were not merely biased, they were, in a technical sense, not very good, and Wall Street knew it and designed products specifically to exploit it.
Take one example, and it is beautifully simple.
The agencies evaluated a pool of mortgages partly by looking at the average credit score of the borrowers.
Average.

So a pool in which every single borrower had a score of six hundred and fifteen, and a pool in which half the borrowers had a score of five hundred and fifty and half had a score of six hundred and eighty, looked identical.
They have the same average.
They have wildly different risk, because the low scoring half will default at a catastrophic rate.
Once the banks understood this, they deliberately constructed pools of dangerous borrowers padded with a few safe ones, engineered to hit the average that produced the rating they wanted.
Take another.

A borrower with no documented income at all was, in some models, treated as less risky than one with documented low income, because the absence of data was scored as neutral rather than as a screaming warning sign.
And a third, which Danny Moses discovered by simply asking.
At a securitisation conference in Las Vegas, he asked an employee of one of the rating agencies what their model predicted would happen if American house prices fell.
The answer was that the model could not accept a negative number.
House price appreciation could be entered as zero, or as a positive figure.
There was no way to enter a decline, because the historical data on which the model was built did not contain one.
Now let me show you the machine that turned this from an ordinary lending disaster into a global catastrophe, because this is the bit most people never get told.
The lowest, riskiest slices of the mortgage bonds, the triple B tranches, were hard to sell.
Nobody wanted the piece that gets wiped out first.
So Wall Street invented a solution.
It gathered up a hundred of these unwanted triple B slices from a hundred different mortgage bonds, put them all in a new pot, and called the pot a collateralised debt obligation, a CDO.
Then it sliced the pot up again into new tranches, and took the resulting product back to the ratings agencies.
And roughly eighty percent of that pot, made entirely out of the worst pieces of the worst bonds, came back rated triple A.
The same rating as government debt.
The justification was diversification.
Spreading risk across a hundred different bonds meant the chances of them all failing at once were small.
That reasoning is fine if the failures are independent, if these are a hundred separate unrelated risks.
But they were not independent at all.
They were a hundred slices of the same bet, on the same borrowers, in the same country, driven by the same interest rates and the same house prices.
If one went, they were all going, for exactly the same reason at exactly the same time.

Lewis's image for this is the one that sticks: it was a machine that took lead and turned it into gold, and the alchemy was performed entirely by the ratings agencies, who were paid by the people bringing them the lead.
And then it got worse, because the market ran out of actual bad loans to package.
Demand for these products exceeded the supply of Americans willing to take out ruinous mortgages.
So the industry invented the synthetic CDO: a CDO made not out of mortgage bonds but out of credit default swaps referencing mortgage bonds.
In other words, a bet on a bet.

That meant the same underlying pool of dodgy loans could be referenced over and over again, so a modest quantity of genuinely bad mortgages could support an enormous multiple of exposure across the system.
This is why the numbers at the end are so much larger than the size of the actual subprime market.
The losses were not limited to the real loans.
They were the real loans multiplied by however many times Wall Street had bet on them.
And who was on the other side?
Two answers, and both are extraordinary.
The first was AIG Financial Products, a small unit in London of one of the world's largest insurance companies, run by a man named Joe Cassano.
AIG had been writing insurance on these products for tiny premiums, on the reasoning that triple A rated instruments essentially never default.
Lewis describes the moment a young employee, Gene Park, decided to actually look at what was inside the deals AIG was insuring, and discovered they were largely subprime mortgages.
He raised it internally.
AIG stopped writing new business at the end of 2005, but by then it had insured tens of billions of dollars of the stuff, and, this is the crucial point, the machine did not stop.
Wall Street simply carried on manufacturing the product and holding the risk itself, because it had grown too profitable to abandon.
The second answer, and this is the part that still astonishes people, is that a very large share of the risk ended up on the balance sheets of the banks that created it.
They were not clever intermediaries offloading danger onto naive customers.
They were the customers.
Lewis's most striking single example is Howie Hubler, a bond trader at Morgan Stanley, who understood perfectly well that the triple B tranches were rubbish and shorted two billion dollars of them.
But paying insurance premiums costs money every year, and to fund those premiums, he sold insurance on around sixteen billion dollars of supposedly safe triple A rated CDOs.
He was right about the small bet and catastrophically wrong about the large one, because the triple A tranches were made of the same material.
His loss, when it landed, was around nine billion dollars, the largest trading loss by a single person in the history of Wall Street.
And Lewis notes that when Hubler left the firm, he was permitted to keep a very large amount of previously deferred pay.
Now, the human part, which is the reason this book reads like a thriller rather than a lecture.
Being right early is indistinguishable from being wrong.
Michael Burry put his fund's money into these bets in 2005.
And then nothing happened.
For two years, nothing happened.
The premiums ticked out of his fund every month.
His performance, on paper, was terrible.

His investors, who had given him money to pick undervalued stocks, discovered that their brilliant stock picker had committed a large portion of their capital to an exotic derivative bet on the American housing market that none of them understood and none of them had agreed to.
They revolted.
They demanded their money back.
They accused him of straying outside his mandate.
Some threatened to sue.

Burry, whose social difficulties made this kind of confrontation close to unbearable, responded by essentially cutting off communication, walling the bets off in a separate structure so investors could not force him to unwind them, and going silent.
He describes the period as the loneliest of his life.

He was, at that stage, in the middle of learning that he had a form of Asperger's syndrome, something he discovered while reading about his own young son's diagnosis, and which explained a great deal about a life spent unable to interpret people while being able to read documents nobody else could stand to read.
Eisman's team had the same experience differently.
They were not doubted by investors so much as by reality.
Through 2006 and into 2007, the loans in the pools were defaulting at rising rates, publicly reported, in the monthly data.
And the prices of the bonds did not move.
Nothing happened.
The market simply declined to acknowledge the information.
Part of the reason was structural.
These securities did not trade on an exchange.
The banks that sold them also decided what they were worth.
If a bank marked its own inventory at a hundred cents, then, officially, the bond was worth a hundred cents, no matter what the underlying loans were doing.

Eisman's team spent months in a state of disbelief, calling around, checking their arithmetic, half convinced they must have misunderstood something fundamental, because it seemed impossible that they could be this right and the market this silent.
And there was a cost to waiting that is easy to skip past when you know how the story ends.
These insurance contracts are not free.
You pay the premium every single month, whether or not anything happens.
Traders call this negative carry, and it is a slow, grinding bleed.
Every month that the world stayed calm, money left the fund and nothing came back.

Lippmann, who was carrying an enormous position at Deutsche Bank and having to justify it internally, described the experience of watching the premiums drain out while his colleagues walked past his desk making remarks.
Lippmann's own position in the story is worth pausing on, because Lewis does not let him off.

He was, simultaneously, telling investors that his own industry's flagship product was worthless, and selling them the instrument that would let them bet against it, and taking a fee for doing so, and holding the same bet himself.
When Eisman's team first met him, their immediate reaction was suspicion: why is a Deutsche Bank salesman knocking on our door telling us the thing his own bank manufactures is rubbish?
What is he not saying?
The answer, when they eventually satisfied themselves about it, was almost disappointing in its simplicity.
He genuinely believed it, and he needed company, because a bet this size requires a market on the other side, and a market requires other people.
Danny Moses put the underlying test bluntly: when a Wall Street salesman is very keen for you to buy something, the first question is not whether the thing is good, it is why he wants you to have it.
In this one instance, the honest answer happened to be one they could live with.
And then, in January 2007, everybody went to Las Vegas.

The American Securitization Forum was the industry's annual conference, and Lewis's account of it is the comic centrepiece of the book, and also the moment the shorts stopped worrying that they had missed something.
Eisman, Vinny and Danny went to meet the people on the other side of their trade, hoping, genuinely, to find someone who could explain why they were wrong.
Instead they found several thousand people in an enormous casino celebrating.
The scene everyone remembers is a dinner where Eisman found himself seated opposite a CDO manager named Wing Chau.
A CDO manager's job was, in theory, to select the assets going into these vehicles and to look after the interests of the investors who bought them.
Eisman asked, straightforwardly, how much of this Chau managed.
The answer was around fifteen billion dollars.
Then Eisman asked the question underneath: how was he paid?
And the answer, as Lewis relates it, was that he was paid on volume.
A fee on the assets under management.
Which meant his incentive was to create more of these things, and that his personal fortunes were essentially unaffected by whether the investors who owned them ever got their money back.
He was a middleman whose incentive was throughput.
Eisman is said to have turned to Danny Moses and said, in effect, whatever he is buying, I want to short it.
Elsewhere in Las Vegas they encountered a lending industry drunk on its own machinery.
Cornwall Capital's people sat through panel discussions in which the general assumption was that everything would continue forever.
And the small human details are what make it real.
Eisman had discovered, back in New York, that his own housekeeper, a woman from Jamaica, had been lent enough money to buy and refinance several houses in Queens with her sister.

In Las Vegas, one of the team met a woman working in a strip club who explained that she owned five houses, each bought with almost no deposit on adjustable rate mortgages, and who was untroubled because prices always went up.
And in the loan documents themselves, the shorts kept finding cases that read like satire.

The most cited is a strawberry picker in Bakersfield, California, a Mexican migrant worker with an annual income of around fourteen thousand dollars, who had been lent something in the region of seven hundred and twenty four thousand dollars to buy a house.
That loan was written, sold, packaged into a bond, sliced, repackaged into a CDO, and a large piece of it was rated triple A.
Cornwall Capital's contribution to all of this deserves its own moment, because it is the smartest single trade in the book.
Ledley, Mai and Hockett worked out that the mispricing was not really in the triple B tranches, which by then everyone was arguing about.
It was higher up.
The double A and triple A tranches of CDOs, the ones considered nearly riskless, could be insured for a tiny annual premium, because everyone believed the rating.
But Cornwall understood that the CDOs were made of correlated material, and that if the bottom went, the top was going with it, only slightly later.
So they bought insurance on the top, where the premium was a fraction of the price, on instruments that would pay out at nearly the same time as the ones everybody else was fighting over.
It was the same bet at a much better price, available only to people who did not believe the labels.
They turned a hundred and ten thousand dollars of starting capital into something north of a hundred million.
Then the thing finally broke.
In early 2007 the index that tracked subprime bonds began to fall, and once it started it did not stop.
In June, two hedge funds run by Bear Stearns, which had loaded up on this material, collapsed.
Through the summer the market seized.
And by 2008 the entire financial system was discovering that it had, in aggregate, taken the same side of the same bet.
Lewis captures the surreality of the end with a scene from a conference in the spring of 2008.
Eisman is on a panel.
A famous and highly respected fund manager is on the same panel, defending Bear Stearns as a solid institution and telling the audience it was a buying opportunity.
And while he is speaking, Eisman is looking at the messages on his handheld device, watching the Bear Stearns share price fall in real time.
He interrupts to tell the room, more or less, that while this gentleman has been speaking, the stock has fallen from around fifty three dollars to around thirty.
Bear Stearns did not exist within days.
And then came the part that ruined the victory for most of them.
They were owed enormous sums by the very banks that were now collapsing.
Their winning bets were only worth something if the counterparty survived to pay.

Ben Hockett's paranoia turned out to be the most practical instinct in the whole story: Cornwall spent the final weeks frantically trying to sell their position to anyone still standing, because a bet against the financial system that pays out only if the financial system remains solvent is not, in the end, a very well designed bet.
They all made money.

Burry's fund returned, over its life from 2000 to the middle of 2008, something like four hundred and eighty nine percent net of fees, against roughly two percent for the broad American stock market over the same period.
He personally made about a hundred million dollars, and made his investors something in the region of seven hundred million.
Eisman's fund made hundreds of millions.
Cornwall made their fortune.
Lippmann made a fortune and a reputation.
And almost none of them enjoyed it.
Lewis is very good on this.
Charlie Ledley, of Cornwall, found the whole experience depressing rather than triumphant.

His reaction to being proved right about the incompetence at the centre of the financial system was not glee but something closer to grief, because he had been operating on an assumption that somewhere in the machine there were adults, and he had just proved conclusively that there were not.
At one stage Cornwall seriously investigated whether one could buy insurance against the failure of the ratings agencies themselves.
Michael Burry, having made an enormous amount of money for people who had spent two years abusing him, received almost no apology, wound down his fund, and withdrew.
Steve Eisman ended up in a strange moral position that Lewis handles with real sympathy.

He had spent his career convinced that the industry he worked in was rotten, and he had now been so thoroughly vindicated that the vindication was worthless, because the cost was borne by millions of people who had never heard of a CDO.
And then Lewis closes the book by going back to his own past, and this is where he tells you what he thinks the moral is.
He has lunch with John Gutfreund, the man who ran Salomon Brothers when Lewis worked there, the man who is the villain of Liar's Poker and who had every reason never to speak to him again.
They are polite.
And Lewis reflects on the single decision that, in his view, set the whole thing in motion, and it happened decades before the mortgages were written.
In 1981, Salomon Brothers became the first Wall Street partnership to convert itself into a public company.
Before that, the firms were partnerships, which meant the people running them were gambling with their own money.
Their houses were on the line.
Every other firm followed.
Once they were public, the calculation changed completely.
The traders and executives took the profits in bonuses each year, and the losses, when they eventually came, fell on shareholders, and finally on taxpayers.
The upside was personal and immediate.
The downside was collective and deferred.
Lewis's line is that no investment bank owned by its own employees would ever have leveraged itself thirty five times over on assets its own leaders did not understand.
It was not that these people were unusually stupid or unusually wicked.
It was that a set of arrangements had been constructed in which nobody who could stop the machine had any personal reason to.
Which points at the deepest idea in the book, and it is why it is worth your time even if you never buy a bond in your life.
The 2008 crisis is usually explained as a failure of intelligence, an inability to model something too complex.
Lewis's evidence says otherwise.
The information was public.
The prospectuses were mailed out.
The default rates were published monthly.
The ratings methodology was known well enough that banks were engineering products to exploit it.
The people who saw it coming did so not through genius, but by reading documents that were available to everyone and asking questions that a child might ask.
What actually failed was incentives, and the willingness to look.

Thousands of clever, well paid people did not look, because their pay depended on not looking, and because everybody around them was not looking either, and because looking would have required them to say something that would have made them, for two long years, look like idiots.
So let me leave you with what you can carry out of it.
First, read the documents.
Whatever the domain, there is almost always a boring, freely available primary source, and almost nobody reads it, and the people who do have a real edge.
Michael Burry's advantage was not intelligence.
It was tolerance for tedium.
Second, follow the incentives before you follow the argument.
When someone tells you something is safe, ask how they are paid, and what happens to them personally if they are wrong.
Wing Chau was paid on volume.
The ratings agencies were paid by the issuers.
The traders were paid annually on paper profits.
Once you know the incentive, the behaviour stops being mysterious.
Third, be suspicious of averages.
The pool that looked identical on its average credit score contained two entirely different populations.
Averages hide exactly the information that matters most, which is the shape of the distribution and where the bodies are buried.
Fourth, ask what the model cannot represent.
The rating agency model could not accept a falling house price.
Every model has a set of outcomes it structurally cannot see, and the important risks live there.
When you are shown a projection, ask what inputs it refuses to take.
Fifth, check whether your diversification is real.
A hundred bets that all depend on the same underlying condition are one bet wearing a hundred hats.
Correlation is the thing that turns a manageable loss into a systemic one.
Sixth, understand that being early looks exactly like being wrong, and plan for it.
Burry was right in 2005 and nearly lost his fund by 2007 because the cost of waiting is real and the social cost of waiting is worse.
If you make a contrarian bet, the important question is not whether you are right, but whether you can survive the period between being right and being seen to be right.
And seventh, remember Ben Hockett's question, which almost nobody asks: if this bet wins, will the person who owes me the money still be able to pay?
A brilliant position with an insolvent counterparty is a piece of paper.

Lewis's final image is of walking through New York after that lunch, past a homeless man asking for money, and reflecting that the entire spectacular machine, the alchemy, the ratings, the billions, all of it, had at the very bottom of the pile a real person in a real house who had been sold a loan he was never going to repay.
Everything above him was built on the assumption that this would not matter.
